summary: Geneve is a flexible overlay encapsulation used to tunnel network traffic. This RFC specifies requirements and a framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in Geneve, meaning active checks for connectivity and faults in these tunnels.

eli5.summary: If a tunnel is made of pipes, you need a way to send a test ball through to see if it's blocked. This describes how to build such checks for Geneve tunnels.

questions: what is the management vni in geneve
why must geneve oam ttl be 255
how does geneve oam use icmp and bfd
subtitle: How to send health-check packets through a Geneve tunnel so they travel the same way real traffic does.

tldr.problem: Operators of Geneve overlay networks need active OAM tests, such as ping or BFD, that experience the same conditions as the traffic they are meant to monitor.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets five requirements for active OAM in Geneve and defines an IP/UDP encapsulation sent over a dedicated Management VNI (default 1), with an inner TTL or Hop Limit of 255.
tldr.outcome: Test packets stay inside the tunnel, are never handed to a tenant, and are dropped by the receiver unless the inner TTL or Hop Limit is 255.

today: RFC 9772 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Geneve Needs Active OAM
sections.content:
Geneve is an overlay protocol that wraps Ethernet, IPv4 or IPv6 traffic and carries metadata with it, as defined in RFC 8926. OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) covers fault management and performance monitoring. Active OAM, in the sense of RFC 7799, uses specially built packets injected into the network. ICMP, ICMPv6, BFD and STAMP are examples.

For a test result to say anything about a Geneve flow, the test packets must share fate with that flow: they must be in-band, crossing the same links and interfaces and getting the same Quality of Service treatment. The monitored object is either a whole Geneve tunnel or one tenant flow inside it.

Tests run between two Geneve tunnel endpoints, called NVEs (Network Virtualization Edges) for simplicity. End-to-end testing between tenants is out of scope, as is any OAM encapsulation other than the IP encapsulation defined here.
sections.eli5: To know if a road has a traffic jam, you send a test car down the same road as everyone else. A test car on a different road would tell you nothing.

sections.title: The Five Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC lists five requirements that any active OAM encapsulation for Geneve has to meet.

  • Requirement 1: test packets MUST share fate with the monitored data, staying in-band and following the same overlay and transport paths in the forward direction.
  • Requirement 2: OAM control messages and data packets MUST be indistinguishable in the underlay network.
  • Requirement 3: Geneve functionality, such as a tunnel endpoint, MUST be able to tell unambiguously that a packet carries OAM.
  • Requirement 4: OAM test packets MUST NOT be forwarded to a tenant system.
  • Requirement 5: there MUST be a way to encode entropy into the underlay forwarding scheme so OAM packets follow the same paths as transit traffic.

Requirement 5 matters because underlay nodes may balance load across several paths using characteristic information in the packet. A test packet that hashes onto a different path would not prove anything about the flow being monitored.
sections.eli5: The test ball must look like a normal ball to everyone along the way, must follow the same route, and must never be handed to the people at the end of the pipe.

sections.title: Two Troubleshooting Cases and the Management VNI
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a Geneve domain where NVE A, NVE B and NVE C connect tenants on VNI 28 and VNI 35. Two cases are considered.

In the first, the Geneve connection between NVE A and NVE C is unstable for every tenant, although the IP underlay forwards correctly. This can be investigated with any VNI value. To satisfy Requirement 4, test packets SHOULD use a VNI that has no tenants. That tunnel is a Geneve control channel and its VNI is the Management VNI. A configured VNI MAY identify it, but the default value 1 is RECOMMENDED.

The control channel MUST NOT carry tenant data. A packet received on it MUST NOT be forwarded to any tenant. It is forwarded if and only if it is sent onto the control channel of the concatenated Geneve tunnel, and otherwise it MUST be terminated locally.

The Management VNI SHOULD be terminated on the tenant-facing side of the Geneve encapsulation and decapsulation functionality, not the data-center-network-facing side. An ICMP echo request is then decapsulated like any other Geneve packet and passed to the NVE's local management function, which generates the echo reply, which is encapsulated in Geneve and sent back. The stated advantage is that repeated echo tests can reveal an intermittent fault in Geneve encap/decap hardware, which a special case at the network-facing side would miss.

In the second case, VNI 35 between NVE A and NVE C suffers problems such as excessive packet loss while the other tunnels are fine. Here the test packet is sent using the VNI of the monitored service flow, so it gets the same treatment as that tenant's packets. RFC 9521 is given as an example for BFD.

ICMP and ICMPv6 provide on-demand defect detection and failure localization. ICMP control messages immediately follow the inner IP header inside Geneve, and ICMP extensions for Geneve networks use the mechanisms of RFC 4884.
sections.eli5: You build a private pipe just for test balls that no family is connected to. If a problem only hits one family, you send the test ball through that family's own pipe instead.

sections.title: IP Encapsulation of Active OAM
sections.content:
Active OAM over the Management VNI uses an IP encapsulation. Protocols such as BFD and STAMP run over UDP, and the destination UDP port in the inner UDP header identifies which OAM protocol is inside. The RFC notes this approach is well known and has been used in MPLS networks (RFC 8029). To use it, the Geneve Protocol Type field MUST be set to 0x0800 (IPv4) or 0x86DD (IPv6).

The inner IP header has strict rules:

  • Destination IP: for IPv4 it MUST be the loopback address 127.0.0.1/32. For IPv6 it MUST come from the Dummy IPv6 Prefix 100:0:0:1::/64 defined in RFC 9780. The IPv6 address is a source-only one, used so the receiver generates an exception and a reply.
  • Source IP: the IP address of the NVE.
  • TTL or Hop Limit: MUST be 255, per RFC 5082. A receiver MUST drop packets whose TTL or Hop Limit is not 255.
sections.eli5: The test ball is put in an envelope addressed to a special mailbox that only the receiving NVE will open, and the envelope carries a seal (255) that proves it was not forwarded from far away.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Active OAM in Geneve inherits the security considerations of RFC 8926. In addition, a system MUST provide a control to limit the rate of Geneve OAM packets punted to the Geneve control plane, so the control plane is not overloaded.

OAM in Geneve uses the General TTL Security Mechanism. Any packet received with an inner TTL or Hop Count other than 255 MUST be discarded. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A guard checks every test ball for the 255 seal and throws away any without it. The guard also limits how many test balls get through at once so the office is not flooded.
